The Omics Hub: Reproducible Bioinformatics & Computational Biology Tutorials

A curated computational biology workbench and open reference library by Dr. Nasir Mahmood Abbasi, PhD. Bridging classical genomics and HPC pipelines with modern AI-augmented research workflows.

Explore Tutorials →

A Practical Learning Environment for Computational Biology

Learn the reasoning behind every workflow.

The Omics Hub helps biologists connect research questions with computational methods. Hands-on labs offer focused exercises; conceptual guides explain scientific choices; advanced templates require adaptation to your inputs and environment; references support lookup and troubleshooting. Choose a lesson format that matches your experience and goal.

01 | Understand

Start with the method

Build the concepts first: files, data formats, quality control, statistics, and the assumptions behind each analysis.

02 | Practice

Practice within the lesson scope

For hands-on labs, follow the stated setup and inspect the exercise outputs. For templates, prepare compatible inputs, adapt the code, and check its behavior before using research data.

03 | Interpret

Connect output to evidence

Learn what a result supports, what it cannot prove, and which decisions require biological and statistical expertise.

New to computational biology? Follow the structured learning path before choosing a specialization.

Start the learning path →

Explore Computational Biology and Bioinformatics

The Omics Hub brings together explanations, focused exercises, and adaptable examples for researchers learning computational methods. Topics range from Linux and High-Performance Computing (HPC) to single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq), metagenomics, and multi-omics. Explore workflow tools such as Nextflow and Snakemake, spatial analysis methods, and the design and limits of AI-assisted research workflows.

Structured Curriculum

What We Cover

Start with computational foundations, then choose a route into genomics, single-cell analysis, or multi-omics. All 58 tutorials remain available as hands-on labs, conceptual guides, advanced templates, or references. Read the learning-format label and prerequisites to understand the lesson scope; exercises may use synthetic fixtures or public data, while templates may require inputs you prepare yourself.

Foundations

Data formats, quality control, statistics, R, Python, Git, and experimental design for bioinformatics.

12 tutorials

Shell scripting, Slurm job scheduling, Conda environments, Snakemake pipelines, and containerization.

10 tutorials

Single-Cell and Spatial

From raw 10X reads to clustering, annotation, trajectory analysis, multi-modal integration, and spatial transcriptomics.

15 tutorials

Omics and AI

Metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, evolutionary genomics, WES pipelines, and AI-driven agentic bioinformatics.

21 tutorials

Why The Omics Hub

The library connects biological questions with computational reasoning. Use each lesson's format, prerequisites, setup notes, and references to judge what it offers and what you need to check in your own environment.

Biological reasoning, not universal cutoffs.

Examples help you interpret diagnostic checks and consider biological context rather than applying a threshold without examining the data.

Learning Example: PBMC 3k QC and Clustering

The scRNA-seq Basics lab starts with a public PBMC 3k count matrix and presents Seurat and Scanpy examples for QC, normalization, clustering, and UMAP. It explains why gene-count and mitochondrial metrics need biological context. This is a focused matrix-to-clustering exercise, not a raw-read processing pipeline or a clinical validation workflow.

Explore the PBMC QC-to-clustering lab →

Check examples in your environment

Where provided, use setup notes, expected outputs, and diagnostic checks to assess an example. Not every biological workflow has been run end to end; verify the relevant steps in your environment before applying them to research data.

Structured Learning Path

The Start Here page suggests a study order and links to foundations and specializations. Check each lesson's prerequisites before moving on.

Built for Biologists

Written for researchers transitioning into computational work. No CS degree assumed. Biological context comes first, code comes second.

Author & educator

Meet the Author: Nasir Mahmood Abbasi, PhD

Computational Biologist & Data Scientist

Welcome to The Omics Hub. I hold a PhD in Cancer Biology and specialise in single-cell multi-omics, cancer genomics, and reproducible computational workflows. I built this platform to help researchers move from biological questions to practical, command-line analysis.

The tutorials focus on practical decisions that arise in research, including Seurat integration, Nextflow pipelines on Slurm, and reference annotation. Each guide is intended to help you understand the analysis and adapt it responsibly to your own data.

Read my full academic journey →
